subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]
passage: In the school garden club, Francis stared at the brown tips on his chilli plant. "Shalini Ma'am, is it dying?" "You tell me. What could cause brown tips?" Francis counted on his fingers. "Maybe it's thirsty. Maybe sunburnt. Or bugs." He pushed a finger into the soil: damp. "Not water." He looked up: the pot sat in shade after noon. "Not sun." Then he crouched and turned over each leaf. Along the stem ran a line of tiny ants. "Pests!" He brushed them off with a twig and set the pot on a saucer of water. Shalini Ma'am nodded.

qa.q: What did Francis find on the stem?
qa.a: He found a line of tiny ants.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he found the ants?
qa.a: Excited and relieved, since checking each cause in turn had led him to the answer.

qa.q: What could Francis do to keep the ants away, and why?
qa.a: He could keep the pot on a saucer of water and check the stem daily, because ants cannot easily cross water.

qa.q: How does Shalini Ma'am see Francis's method?
qa.a: Shalini Ma'am approves, as her nod shows, since Francis found the cause by reasoning himself.

grounding: A boy asks why a plant is failing, checks water, sun and pests in turn, and finds ants on the stem.

subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]
passage: I'm Omkar, and I work next to Sahil in the school garden period. Last Tuesday his chilli plant had brown tips on nearly every leaf. He crouched down and said, out loud, "Not enough water? Sun too strong? Or bugs?" He pushed a finger into the soil: damp, so not water. He looked up at the sky: our bed gets shade after eleven, so probably not sun. Then he turned the leaves over one by one. Low on the stem there was a line of tiny black ants going up and down. He fetched a cup of soapy water from the garden teacher, wiped the stem and pushed the ant trail away with a stick. I don't know if he was worried, but he checked that plant every break for the rest of the week.

qa.q: What did Sahil find on the stem?
qa.a: A line of tiny black ants going up and down.

qa.q: What might Sahil have been feeling about the plant?
qa.a: He was probably worried, since he checked it every break for the rest of the week.

qa.q: What else could Sahil try if the tips keep browning?
qa.a: Ask the garden teacher and keep checking one cause at a time, the same careful way he ruled out water and sun.

qa.q: How does Omkar see Sahil's checking?
qa.a: Omkar notes each step Sahil took but admits not knowing whether Sahil was worried.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy test each possible cause of a sick plant and find ants on the stem.

subtype: Approach: figuring out why the plant is dying [Thinking]
passage:
Monday: Omkar noticed brown tips on the curry-leaf plant by the front door. His sister Avni said, "It's thirsty." Omkar wasn't sure. He wrote three questions on a sticky note: Water? Sun? Insects?
Wednesday: After school he checked the soil. Moist, not dry. He watched the pot at noon: sun for only an hour. That left one question. He borrowed Papa's reading glasses and a torch and peered at the stem. Ants, dozens of them, marching up to tiny white spots under the leaves.
Saturday: He had washed the stem with water every day and drawn a ring of chalk round the pot. The ants were gone. The new leaves came out plain green. Avni admitted, "Okay, not thirsty."

qa.q: What three questions did Omkar write?
Why didn't Omkar just water the plant?
qa.a: He felt unsure Avni was right and wanted to check each possible cause first.

qa.q: What else could Omkar do if the ants come back?
qa.a: Keep watching the stem and ask at a nursery about the white spots, since the ants may be visiting them.
Avni first says the plant is thirsty, and by Saturday admits it wasn't.

grounding: Over a week, a boy checks water, sun and pests in turn and finds ants causing his plant's brown tips.
